questions.stem: Which is correct about Diphtheria membrane?

options.label: A
options.text: Grey membrane that bleeds on removal

options.label: B
options.text: Grey membrane that does not bleed on removal

options.label: C
options.text: Grey pseudo-membrane that bleeds on removal

options.label: D
options.text: Grey pseudo-membrane that does not bleed on removal

questions.answerText: Grey pseudo-membrane that bleeds on removal
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Grey pseudo-membrane that bleeds on removal

 

Diphtheria is caused by Corynebacterium diphtheriae, which produces a grey-colored pseudomembrane over the tonsils. This pseudomembrane forms as a result of bacterial infection and tissue necrosis. The term "pseudo" indicates that the membrane appears like a real membrane but is not firmly attached. If an attempt is made to remove this pseudomembrane, it will bleed. The bleeding occurs because the membrane is not entirely separate from the underlying tissue, which distinguishes it from a true membrane that could be removed without causing bleeding.

 

 

Educational Objective:


A diphtheria pseudomembrane is grey in color and bleeds if attempts are made to remove it.

 

Note : 

 

  • Diphtheria affects three  systems: the heart (causing carditis), the nerves (causing neuritis), and the adrenal glands (causing adrenal hemorrhage).
  • Diphtheria is caused by a toxin produced by Corynebacterium diphtheriae, not by the bacteria itself.
  • The pseudomembrane associated with diphtheria is caused by the bacteria, not the toxin. The treatment of choice for diphtheria is antitoxin, as the disease is toxin mediated.
  • Antibiotics, such as erythromycin, are used to kill the bacteria and prevent further toxin production. However, antibiotics cannot neutralize the toxin already present in the bloodstream.

questions.stem: Metachromatic granules can be stained by:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Albert stain

 

 

Metachromatic granules are special granules present at the ends (poles) of certain bacteria, giving them names like "polar granules." They appear bluish or violet in color, which is why they are called "metachromatic"—meta means a change in color, specifically a bluish-violet appearance. These granules were discovered by a scientist named Babes, which is why they are also referred to as Babes-Ernst granules. Additionally, they are known as "volutin granules" because they were first discovered in Spirillum volutans.

 

These granules are primarily made up of phosphate and tend to appear when bacteria face conditions of nutrient deprivation or starvation. In such situations, bacteria store phosphate in these granules. There are four stains that can be used to visualize metachromatic granules, remembered by the mnemonic "PLAN," where P stands for Ponder stain, L stands for Loeffler’s methylene blue, A stands for Albert stain (which is the answer to this question), and N stands for Neisser stain.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Gram stain: This is incorrect because it is not part of the four stains mentioned for staining metachromatic granules. The mnemonic "PLAN" does not include Gram stain.

 

Option C. Gram-negative stain: This is incorrect as it is not one of the stains that highlight metachromatic granules. Instead, it is used for general bacterial differentiation.

 

Option D. Prussian blue: This option is incorrect since Prussian blue is not included in the mnemonic "PLAN" for metachromatic granule stains. Instead, Albert stain is the correct choice.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Metachromatic granules are bluish-violet granules that appear at the poles of certain bacteria and are stained using specific stains like Albert stain. They are also known as Babes-Ernst granules, volutin granules, or polar bodies.

questions.stemHtml: Identify the organism:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Nocardia species

 

The image shows a branching, filamentous structure that closely resembles hyphae, a feature typical of certain bacteria that appear similar to fungi. Both Nocardia and Actinomyces species exhibit this branching, filamentous appearance. However, the key distinguishing factor here is the color of the staining:

 

 

Nocardia is an acid-fast organism, meaning it retains the red stain in an acid-fast stain test.

 

Since the image displays a red color, it indicates that the organism is acid-fast, leading to the identification of Nocardia species 

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Actinomyces species: Actinomyces also shows branching filamentous structures similar to Nocardia. However, it is not acid-fast and would appear blue if stained using acid-fast methods. The red coloration in the image excludes this option.

 

Option C. Mycobacterium tuberculosis: While this bacterium is acid-fast, it does not typically display the branching, filamentous structure shown in the image. Instead, it appears as rod-shaped bacilli.

 

Option D. Mycobacterium leprae: This bacterium is also acid-fast but does not exhibit the filamentous, branching structure observed in the image. It typically appears as straight or slightly curved rods.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Nocardia species is characterized by its branching, filamentous structure and its ability to retain red staining in acid-fast tests.

questions.stem: Lysogenic conversion is:

options.label: A
options.text: Integration of host bacterial nucleic acid to phage

options.label: B
options.text: Integration of phage nucleic acid to host bacteria genome

options.label: C
options.text: Bacterial mechanism to cause antigenic shift

questions.answerText: Integration of phage nucleic acid to host bacteria genome
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Integration of phage nucleic acid to host bacteria genome

 

Lysogenic conversion occurs when a bacteriophage, which is a virus that infects bacteria, integrates its genetic material into the bacterial genome. In this process, the phage DNA becomes incorporated into the bacterial DNA and remains dormant as a prophage. This integration allows the phage DNA to be replicated along with the bacterial genome during cell division. The bacterium can acquire new traits through this process, which may include toxin production or changes in other phenotypic characteristics, altering the bacterial cell's properties.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Integration of host bacterial nucleic acid to phage: This option is incorrect as lysogenic conversion specifically refers to the integration of phage DNA into the bacterial genome, not the other way around.

 

Option C. Bacterial mechanism to cause antigenic shift: Antigenic shift is typically associated with changes in surface proteins of viruses, such as influenza, and not directly with the process of lysogenic conversion.

 

Option D. Bacterial method to acquire resistance: While lysogenic conversion can result in new bacterial traits, such as toxin production, it is not specifically a mechanism for acquiring antibiotic resistance. Resistance is more often acquired through other mechanisms like plasmid-mediated conjugation.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Lysogenic conversion involves the integration of bacteriophage genetic material into the bacterial genome, leading to potential changes in the bacterium's traits.

questions.stemHtml: Microscopic picture of stool sample of a patient is given. What is the mode of transmission of the parasite?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Feco-oral transmission

 

 

The image shows an egg with a characteristic barrel shape and a mucous plug at each pole. These features are typical of Trichuris trichiura, also known as the whipworm. The transmission of Trichuris trichiura occurs through the feco-oral route. The eggs are released in the feces of infected individuals, and when contaminated food or water is ingested, the eggs are introduced into a new host. Inside the host, the eggs hatch and develop into larvae in the intestine.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Ingestion of undercooked beef: This is the mode of transmission for infections like Taenia saginata (beef tapeworm), not Trichuris trichiura. Trichuris does not involve transmission through meat consumption.

 

Option C. Penetration by filariform larvae: This option is incorrect because filariform larvae are associated with infections like Strongyloides stercoralis and hookworms, not whipworms.

 

Option D. Penetration by rhabditiform larvae: Rhabditiform larvae are typically related to Strongyloides stercoralis. They are not involved in the transmission of Trichuris trichiura.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The transmission of Trichuris trichiura occurs via the feco-oral route, where contaminated food or water leads to ingestion of eggs that hatch in the host's intestine.

questions.stem: In Robertson cooked meat media, meat color will change to:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Red 

 

Robertson's Cooked Meat (RCM) medium is used for cultivating anaerobic bacteria. It contains nutrient broth and pieces of cooked meat, usually from ox heart, submerged in liquid paraffin to create an anaerobic environment. During bacterial growth, especially by anaerobes, the meat undergoes a reduction process, which changes its color. This reduction typically results in the meat turning red. The red color indicates active bacterial metabolism in the medium, making it a useful indicator of anaerobic bacterial growth.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Pink: Although some color changes can occur, the typical outcome in RCM broth due to reduction is a red color rather than pink.

 

Option C. Blue: A blue color change is not associated with the reactions occurring in RCM broth. Blue would suggest the presence of oxygen or pH changes, which are not characteristic of this medium.

 

Option D. No color change: Anaerobic bacterial growth in the medium causes a reduction reaction, leading to a visible color change. Thus, no color change would indicate a lack of bacterial activity, which is not typical when anaerobes are present.

 

Educational Objective:

 

In Robertson Cooked Meat medium, anaerobic bacterial growth causes a reduction reaction that changes the meat color to red, indicating active metabolism.

questions.stemHtml: The following picture of an egg belongs to:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Necator americanus

 

The image shows an egg that is non-bile stained, transparent, and contains a segmented ovum with four blastomeres. This is characteristic of hookworm eggs, which include Ancylostoma duodenale and Necator americanus. The two types of hookworm eggs appear identical under the microscope, and differentiation between them cannot be made based solely on egg morphology. Since Necator americanus is provided as an option here, Hookworm infections are typically diagnosed by identifying these eggs in stool samples.

 

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Ascaris lumbricoides: The eggs of Ascaris lumbricoides are typically round or oval, have a thick, bumpy outer shell, and are bile-stained. They do not contain multiple blastomeres like the egg shown in the image.

 

Option B. Enterobius vermicularis: The eggs of Enterobius vermicularis (pinworm) are oval, flattened on one side, and contain a larva inside, not the segmented blastomeres seen in the image.

 

Option D. Trichuris trichiura: The eggs of Trichuris trichiura (whipworm) are barrel-shaped with prominent plugs at each pole, which differs significantly from the appearance of the egg in the image.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The presence of non-bile stained, transparent eggs with four blastomeres is indicative of hookworm species like Necator americanus or Ancylostoma duodenale.

questions.stem: Lancefield classification is done on the basis of:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) C-substance

 

Lancefield classification is a system used to categorize beta-hemolytic Streptococci based on the presence of specific carbohydrate antigens in their cell walls. These carbohydrate antigens, known as the C-substance or C-carbohydrate, form the basis of this classification. The groups are labeled A through V (excluding I and J) depending on the type of C-carbohydrate present. This classification helps identify various Streptococcus species, such as Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A), which plays a significant role in human infections.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Glycoprotein O: This option is incorrect because glycoprotein O is not used for Lancefield classification. Glycoproteins are typically involved in other cellular functions and recognition processes, not specifically in classifying streptococcal species.

 

Option C. Muramic acid: Muramic acid is a component of bacterial peptidoglycan, contributing to the structure of the bacterial cell wall, but it is not used in the Lancefield classification.

 

Option D. Antibiotic resistance: While antibiotic resistance is a crucial factor in the clinical treatment of infections, it does not play a role in the Lancefield classification of Streptococci.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The Lancefield classification system is based on the presence of specific C-carbohydrate antigens in the cell walls of beta-hemolytic Streptococci.

questions.stem: Bacillus anthracis is:

options.label: B
options.text: Gram positive rods with square ends

options.label: C
options.text: Gram positive bacilli with spherical ends

questions.answerText: Gram positive rods with square ends
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Gram-positive rods with square ends

 

Bacillus anthracis is a Gram-positive, rod-shaped bacterium that is distinctive for its square-ended appearance. It is often arranged in long chains, resembling a "bamboo-stick" appearance under the microscope. The bacterium is non-motile, encapsulated with a polypeptide (poly-D-glutamic acid) capsule, and capable of forming spores. The square ends and the characteristic arrangement help in differentiating Bacillus anthracis from other bacilli. Its Gram-positive nature means that it retains the crystal violet stain and appears purple under a microscope.

 

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Gram-positive cocci in cluster: This describes bacteria like Staphylococcus, not Bacillus anthracis. Bacillus anthracis is rod-shaped, not spherical.

 

Option C. Gram-positive bacilli with spherical ends: While this is closer to the correct family of bacteria, Bacillus anthracis specifically has square ends rather than spherical ones.

 

Option D. Gram-negative cocci in cluster: This option is incorrect because Bacillus anthracis is Gram-positive, not Gram-negative, and is rod-shaped rather than cocci.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Bacillus anthracis is identified as a Gram-positive, rod-shaped bacterium with square ends and a bamboo-stick arrangement.

questions.stem: When should you perform the Widal test in a case of Typhoid?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) 2nd week

 

The Widal test is a serological test used to diagnose typhoid fever by detecting antibodies against Salmonella typhi and Salmonella paratyphi antigens (O and H antigens). Antibodies typically start to appear in the patient's blood during the 2nd week of infection. Performing the test in the 2nd week is crucial for accurate results, as this is when the antibody titers are most likely to be detectable. Testing earlier, such as in the 1st week, would yield inaccurate results since antibodies have not yet developed to detectable levels.

questions.stem: Out of 20 children that went to the party, 11 developed abdominal pain, diarrhea with nausea and vomiting around 4 hours after food intake. Most likely causative agent:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Staphylococcus

 

 

The symptoms described, such as the onset of nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain within 4 hours of food intake, suggest food poisoning due to a preformed toxin. Staphylococcus aureus is known for causing rapid-onset food poisoning, typically within 2-6 hours after ingestion of contaminated food. The toxins produced by Staphylococcus stimulate the vagus nerve and the vomiting center in the brain, leading to these symptoms. Common sources include dairy products, meat, and improperly stored or prepared foods.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Rota virus: This option is incorrect as rotavirus typically causes gastroenteritis with a longer incubation period, usually 24-48 hours, rather than the rapid onset seen here.

 

Option C. Streptococcus: Streptococcal infections are not commonly associated with rapid-onset food poisoning. They are more likely to cause infections like pharyngitis and skin infections.

 

Option D. Clostridium perfringens: This bacterium can cause food poisoning, but the symptoms usually develop after 8-16 hours of ingestion, not the rapid 4-hour onset described in this case.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Food poisoning with rapid onset of symptoms (2-6 hours) after ingestion is often caused by Staphylococcus aureus, due to its preformed enterotoxins.

questions.stem: HUS is caused by:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) O157: H7 of EHEC

 

Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome (HUS) is caused by a specific serotype of Escherichia coli known as O157: H7. This serotype belongs to the Enterohemorrhagic E. coli (EHEC) group. EHEC is one of the six types of E. coli studied, and while all these types cause diarrhea, EHEC has unique characteristics. Apart from diarrhea, EHEC causes two additional conditions: HUS (Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome) and hemorrhagic colitis. The association of EHEC with these conditions is due to its ability to produce virotoxins, which lead to the characteristic symptoms of both HUS and hemorrhagic colitis.

 

In particular, the O157: H7 serotype of EHEC is notable for causing these serious complications. To differentiate this strain from others, a laboratory technique using sorbitol MacConkey agar is used. Unlike other strains of E. coli, O157: H7 does not ferment sorbitol, making it distinguishable when grown on sorbitol MacConkey agar. This diagnostic method is crucial for identifying EHEC in clinical settings.

 

Other Options:


Option A. O157: H7 of EIEC: Enteroinvasive E. coli (EIEC) is associated with invasive diarrhea but is not linked to HUS or hemorrhagic colitis.
 

Option B. O157: H7 of EPEC: Enteropathogenic E. coli (EPEC) primarily causes diarrhea, especially in infants, but it does not cause HUS.
 

Option C. O157: H7 of ETEC: Enterotoxigenic E. coli (ETEC) is known for causing traveler's diarrhea but is not associated with HUS. The mnemonic T for T refers to toxigenic and traveler's diarrhea.

 

Educational Objective:
 

Enterohemorrhagic E. coli (EHEC) serotype O157: H7 is specifically responsible for causing Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome (HUS) and hemorrhagic colitis, in addition to diarrhea.

questions.stem: Gas gangrene is caused by:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Clostridium perfringens

 

 

Gas gangrene is primarily caused by Clostridium perfringens, a unique, gas-forming bacterium. Unlike most bacteria that ferment sugars to produce only acid, Clostridium perfringens ferments sugar to produce both acid and gas. This dual production is what leads to the characteristic symptoms of gas gangrene.

 

In a typical scenario, such as a road traffic accident, a person may sustain a wound that becomes contaminated with Clostridium perfringens spores from the soil. When these spores enter the wound, the bacteria start to grow by fermenting glucose present in the blood of the affected area. The fermentation process produces acid, which leads to tissue necrosis (gangrene), and gas, which accumulates within the gangrenous tissue, creating bubbles and a characteristic crackling sensation known as crepitus.

 

The condition is called gas gangrene because the gangrenous tissue contains gas produced by the bacterial activity. Clostridium perfringens is the most well-known cause, but other species like Clostridium septicum and Clostridium novyi can also cause gas gangrene. 

 

Mnemonic "Punjab Se Nagpur": 

 

P for perfringens, 

 

S for septicum,

 

N for novyi. 

 

Other Options:


Option B. Bacillus cereus: This is incorrect. Bacillus cereus is typically associated with food poisoning rather than causing gas gangrene. It does not ferment sugars to produce gas in the way Clostridium species do.
 

Option C. Helicobacter pylori: Incorrect. Helicobacter pylori is associated with gastric ulcers and chronic gastritis but has no role in causing gas gangrene.
 

Option D. Treponema pallidum: Incorrect. Treponema pallidum is the causative agent of syphilis and is not involved in gas gangrene formation.

 

Educational Objective:


Clostridium perfringens is the primary bacterium responsible for gas gangrene, producing both acid and gas during glucose fermentation, leading to tissue necrosis and gas accumulation in affected areas.

questions.stemHtml: A female from Himachal Pradesh presented with verrucous lesion growth on the skin with the following microscopic finding. Identify the agent:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Chromoblastomycosis

 

The image shows brown, septate fungal bodies that resemble copper pennies, which are also known as sclerotic bodies or Medlar bodies. This characteristic appearance is a hallmark of Chromoblastomycosis, a chronic fungal infection.

 

The condition typically presents with verrucous (warty) lesions, The patient's location in Himachal Pradesh and the mention of a verrucous lesion align with typical cases of chromoblastomycosis in certain endemic regions.

 

The condition is specifically identified by these copper-colored, brown septate bodies seen on a skin biopsy, making chromoblastomycosis The image is crucial in diagnosing this condition as it displays the characteristic sclerotic bodies.

 

 

Other Options:


Option A. Blastomycosis: This is incorrect because blastomycosis typically presents with broad-based budding yeast in tissue and does not show the characteristic sclerotic bodies (copper penny appearance).
 

Option B. Pheohyphomycosis: This condition involves dematiaceous (pigmented) fungi, but it does not specifically present with the copper-colored sclerotic bodies that are seen in chromoblastomycosis.
 

Option C. Sporotrichosis: This is incorrect as sporotrichosis typically presents with linear ulcerative lesions following lymphatic pathways, often after a rose thorn prick. The characteristic finding on biopsy is an asteroid or cigar body, not a copper-colored sclerotic body.

 

 

 

Educational Objective:

 

Chromoblastomycosis is identified by verrucous lesions and brown, septate fungal bodies (sclerotic bodies or Medlar bodies) resembling copper pennies on biopsy.

questions.stem: Anchovy Sauce pus/chocolate brown pus is the clinical feature of:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Amoebic liver abscess

 

Amoebic liver abscess, caused by the protozoan Entamoeba histolytica, is characterized by brown, anchovy sauce-like pus. Infection occurs when contaminated food or water is ingested, introducing the cysts into the intestines. These cysts release trophozoites, which invade the intestinal wall, forming ulcers and causing symptoms like diarrhea, dysentery, and abdominal pain. The trophozoites can reach the liver through the portal vein, forming an abscess. If untreated, the infection can spread to the lungs, leading to further abscess formation. 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

Other Options:


Option B. Pyogenic liver abscess: This is incorrect because pyogenic abscesses contain yellow or greenish pus caused by bacterial infections, not the characteristic brown anchovy sauce-like pus.


Option C. Peritoneal abscess: This is incorrect as peritoneal abscesses do not typically produce anchovy sauce-like pus; they are often secondary to other infections and present with different features.


Option D. Hydatid liver: This is incorrect because hydatid cysts, caused by Echinococcus species, typically contain clear, watery fluid and not the characteristic brown pus seen in amoebic liver abscess.

 

Educational Objective:


Anchovy sauce-like pus is a hallmark feature of an amoebic liver abscess caused by Entamoeba histolytica and results from the necrosis of liver tissue due to invasive trophozoites.

questions.stemHtml: A young woman presents with progressive dyspnea for 3 months. A cavitatory lesion was detected in the right lower lobe of the lung and lobectomy was performed. Histopathological picture is given. Most likely cause of the disease and the number of layers seen in the wall:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Echinococcus with 3 layers

 

A cavitary lung lesion with a three-layered structure is characteristic of a hydatid cyst caused by Echinococcus granulosus, also known as the dog tapeworm. This parasite forms cysts in various organs, including the lungs. The cyst's three layers are:

 

  1. Pericyst: The outer layer from host tissue.
  2. Ectocyst: A firm, protective cuticular layer.
  3. Endocyst: The innermost layer, producing brood capsules containing protoscolices, which can develop into adult tapeworms if ingested by a host
  4.  

 

Other Options:


Option B. Strongyloides with 2 layers: This is incorrect because Strongyloides stercoralis causes pulmonary symptoms through autoinfection and migration of larvae, but it does not form a three-layered cyst in the lungs.


Option C. Paragonimus with 3 layers: Paragonimus westermani is associated with lung infections and cavitary lesions, but it does not produce a three-layered cyst like Echinococcus. The cyst structure in Paragonimus is different and not as complex as that of Echinococcus.
 

Option D. Cysticercosis with 2 layers: This is incorrect because Cysticercosis, caused by Taenia solium, involves the formation of cysticerci in tissues like the brain or muscles, but it does not involve a three-layered cyst structure.

 

Educational Objective:


The three-layered structure (pericyst, ectocyst, endocyst) is a characteristic feature of hydatid cysts caused by Echinococcus granulosus.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a non-motile bacteria?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Klebsiella pneumoniae

 

Klebsiella pneumoniae, it does not possess flagella for movement and is therefore non-motile.

 

 

Motility in bacteria is primarily due to the presence of flagella, which are structures that enable them to move. Bacteria with flagella can be classified based on the arrangement of their flagella, such as polar (flagella emerging from one or both poles of the cell) or peritrichous (flagella spread across the entire surface).

 

Motile with polar flagella:

 

  • Very Polar Solution HCL 
  • Vibrio
  • Pseudomonas
  • Spirochetes
  • H.pylori
  • Campylobacter

Motile with peritrichous flagella:

 

  • Cute Baby SLEP
  • Clostridia all except cl.perfringens
  • Bacillus except b.antrax
  • Salmonella except salmonella gallenarum – pullorum
  • Listeria monocytogen
  • E.Coli
  • Proteus

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Helicobacter pylori is also motile due to polar flagella, which help it move through the stomach lining.

 

Option C. Vibrio cholerae is motile with polar flagella, allowing it to swim through aquatic environments. 

 

Option D. E. coli is identified as motile due to its peritrichous flagella, meaning it has flagella spread around its body.

 

Educational Objective:


Klebsiella pneumoniae is a non-motile bacterium because it lacks flagella, making it unable to move like other motile bacteria such as E. coli, Helicobacter pylori, and Vibrio cholerae.

  1. Gram-positive cocci in chains: The bacteria appear as circular (cocci) and are arranged in chains. They are Gram-positive as they retain the violet color during the Gram staining process. This is a hallmark characteristic of Streptococcus species.

Pike’s media as a transport media: Pike's media is used as a transport medium for Streptococcus pyogenes because this bacterium is delicate and requires careful handling to survive transport without contamination. Streptolysin S, produced by Streptococcus pyogenes, is an oxygen-stable hemolysin, while Streptolysin O is oxygen-labile. Understanding the characteristics of bacterial toxins is crucial for identifying and differentiating Streptococcus infections.

questions.stem: Blood culture of a patient shows growth of gram-positive cocci which are catalase-positive and coagulase-negative. The patient was on a CVP line last week. The most likely etiological agent is?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Staphylococcus epidermidis

 

 

The organism is a gram-positive cocci, which can be categorized into two main groups: Staphylococcus and Streptococcus. Since it is catalase-positive, it belongs to the Staphylococcus group, as Streptococcus and Enterococcus are catalase-negative. The coagulase test further differentiates Staphylococcus species: Staphylococcus aureus is coagulase-positive, while other species, including Staphylococcus epidermidis, are coagulase-negative. The patient's history of a recent CVP line placement suggests Staphylococcus epidermidis, a common cause of infections related to such lines. Thus, the clinical context and lab findings indicate Staphylococcus epidermidis as the most likely etiological agent.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Staphylococcus aureus is ruled out because it is coagulase-positive, while the question specifies a coagulase-negative result.
 

Option C. Streptococcus pyogenes is incorrect because it is a catalase-negative organism, and the question specifies a catalase-positive one.
 

Option D. Enterococcus faecalis is also incorrect, as Enterococcus species are a type of gamma Streptococcus and are catalase-negative. Additionally, they are not the primary cause of infections related to CVP lines.

 

Educational Objective:

 

In patients with a history of CVP line placement, when gram-positive cocci that are catalase-positive and coagulase-negative are identified, Staphylococcus epidermidis is the most likely causative agent.

questions.stem: A patient presented with some unknown fungal infection. Microscopic examination revealed brown-colored spherical fungi with septate hyphae. Possible condition:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Chromoblastomycosis

 

A fungal infection characterized by brown-colored spherical fungi with septate hyphae is most consistent with chromoblastomycosis. The description of brown color and septate structure matches the classic presentation of this condition. These fungi often appear as “copper pennies” under the microscope due to their dark pigmentation and distinctive shape. The presence of septate hyphae further supports the diagnosis of chromoblastomycosis, which is known for its characteristic microscopic appearance.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Histoplasmosis: Incorrect because it typically presents with small intracellular yeast cells rather than brown, spherical fungi. It does not feature septate hyphae.


Option C. Coccidioidomycosis: Incorrect because its microscopic examination usually shows spherules with endospores, not brown-colored, septate fungi.


Option D. Candida albicans: Incorrect because it presents as yeast cells or pseudohyphae and does not exhibit the dark, brown, spherical structures seen in chromoblastomycosis.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Chromoblastomycosis is diagnosed by the presence of brown, spherical fungi with septate hyphae, often described as resembling “copper pennies” in appearance under the microscope. This characteristic appearance is key for identifying the condition.

questions.stemHtml: A known HIV-infected patient develops diarrhea. Fecal examination shows Isospora belli. He was treated with TMP-SMX. Diarrhea subsided, but fever persisted. Bone marrow examination showed the following picture with an intracellular fungus. Which of the following is not true?

options.label: A
options.text: It cannot be grown in SDA

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Does not cause disseminated disease

 

In this case, the patient, who is known to be HIV-positive, initially presented with diarrhea caused by Isospora belli, which responded to treatment with TMP-SMX (trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole). Although the diarrhea resolved, the patient’s fever persisted, suggesting another underlying cause. A bone marrow examination revealed the presence of a fungus inside macrophages, as seen in the image. This observation is characteristic of Histoplasma capsulatum, which is known for being an intracellular fungus that resides within macrophages.

 

Histoplasmosis is a systemic fungal infection, and in immunocompromised patients such as those with HIV, it can progress to disseminated disease, affecting multiple organs beyond the lungs. The ability of Histoplasma to cause disseminated infection makes statement D incorrect, as it is false to state that it does not cause such infections.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. It cannot be grown in SDA: This statement is true because Histoplasma primarily resides inside host cells, making it difficult to culture directly on media like SDA (Sabouraud Dextrose Agar) without special handling.

 

Option B. Spores are the infective form: This is also correct. The spores of Histoplasma are the form that can be inhaled, leading to infection initially through the lungs.

 

Option C. It is an intracellular pathogen: This statement is true and aligns with the observed presence of Histoplasma inside macrophages. It is well-known for its ability to survive within the phagocytic cells of the host.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Histoplasma capsulatum is an intracellular fungus that can cause disseminated infections in immunocompromised individuals, such as those with HIV. It can be identified microscopically by its presence inside macrophages and is not easily cultured on standard fungal media.

questions.stem: Which is correct about the larval stage of Taenia solium?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Cysticercus cellulosae

 

The larval stage of Taenia solium is called Cysticercus cellulosae. This stage develops when a human ingests eggs of Taenia solium, leading to the development of larvae in various tissues. These larvae, also known as cysticerci, form cyst-like structures, often in muscles, brain, and other tissues, leading to a condition called cysticercosis. The term "cellulosae" refers to the tissue (often muscle or connective tissue) where these cysticerci can embed and develop.

 

 

 

 

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Larva currens: Incorrect. This term is associated with Strongyloides stercoralis infections, not with Taenia solium. It describes a rapidly moving larval track seen in the skin, which is not related to the life cycle of Taenia solium.


Option C. Cutaneous larva migrans: Incorrect. This is a term used for the skin condition caused by the migration of larvae of Ancylostoma species (hookworms). It is not related to Taenia solium.


Option D. Visceral larva migrans: Incorrect. This term is used to describe infections caused by larvae of Toxocara species, which migrate through various internal organs, causing symptoms like fever and organ inflammation. It does not apply to the larval stage of Taenia solium.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The larval stage of Taenia solium is Cysticercus cellulosae, which can cause cysticercosis when humans ingest Taenia eggs, leading to the development of cysts in tissues like muscle and the central nervous system.

questions.stem: Classical complement activated by:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Ag – Ab complex

 

The classical complement pathway is triggered by the presence of an antigen-antibody (Ag-Ab) complex in the blood. This means that the pathway gets activated only when an antigen (foreign substance) binds with an antibody, forming a complex. It is specifically initiated by antibodies like IgG or IgM bound to antigens. Once the Ag-Ab complex is present, C1 is the first complement component to become activated, leading to a cascade of reactions that involve other complement proteins such as C4, C2, and eventually C3 and beyond.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. C1. Incorrect as the initial step in the classical pathway involves the presence of an Ag-Ab complex, which then activates C1. C1 alone is not the trigger but rather a component that follows the Ag-Ab interaction.

 

Option B. C3 convertase. Incorrect because this is an enzyme complex formed later in the complement cascade and is not responsible for initiating the classical pathway.

 

Option C. IgA. Incorrect since the classical pathway is typically activated by IgG or IgM antibodies, not IgA.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The classical complement pathway is activated by the presence of antigen-antibody complexes, specifically involving IgG or IgM. This activation then triggers the complement protein C1 to start the cascade.

questions.stemHtml: Lung biopsy of a neutropenic patient shows the following organism on staining. Identify the organism:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Aspergillus

 

In a neutropenic patient, the likelihood of opportunistic fungal infections increases. The image provided shows narrow, septate hyphae with acute angle branching (approximately 45 degrees), which is characteristic of Aspergillus species. Aspergillus is known for its ability to form septate hyphae and branching at acute angles. 

 

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Mucor and D. Rhizopus: Incorrect because these fungi are part of the Mucorales group, which typically present with broad, non-septate hyphae and right-angle (90-degree) branching. These features are different from what is observed in the image provided, where the hyphae are narrow and septate.

 

Option C. Penicillium: Incorrect because it has a distinct conidial structure that does not match the image. It does not typically present with the acute angle branching and septate hyphae seen in Aspergillus.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Aspergillus is characterized by narrow, septate hyphae with acute (45-degree) branching, making it a common cause of opportunistic infections, especially in neutropenic patients. It is important to differentiate it from Mucor and Rhizopus, which have broad, non-septate hyphae with right-angle branching.

questions.stem: Tetanus toxin acts by:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Presynaptic blocking

 

 

Tetanus toxin, also known as tetanospasmin, acts by presynaptic inhibition of GABA (gamma-aminobutyric acid) and glycine release. GABA and glycine are inhibitory neurotransmitters in the central nervous system that facilitate muscle relaxation. The toxin binds to the presynaptic terminals of inhibitory neurons, preventing the release of these neurotransmitters. As a result, inhibitory signaling is blocked, leading to uncontrolled muscle contractions due to unopposed excitatory signals. This mechanism is responsible for the characteristic muscle spasms and rigidity seen in tetanus, including complications like trismus (lockjaw) and opisthotonus (arched back posture).

 

Botulinum toxin’ (BT)

 

  • After entry (either ingested, inhaled, or produced in a wound).
  • Transported via blood to peripheral cholinergic nerve terminals.
  • Binds to acetylcholine receptors at neuromuscular junction. 
  • Blockage of release of the acetylcholine.
  • Flaccid paralysis.

 

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Blocking gamma motor neurons: Incorrect because tetanus toxin specifically targets inhibitory interneurons, not directly affecting gamma motor neurons.

 

Option B. Blocking muscle end plate receptor: Incorrect as the toxin acts at the level of the presynaptic neuron, not at the muscle end plate itself.


Option C. Blocking Ach release: Incorrect for tetanus toxin; this mechanism describes the action of botulinum toxin, which inhibits the release of acetylcholine (Ach) at the neuromuscular junction, leading to flaccid paralysis rather than muscle rigidity.

 

 

 

Educational Objective:

 

Tetanus toxin causes presynaptic inhibition of GABA and glycine, leading to uncontrolled muscle contraction and spastic paralysis. This is distinct from the mechanism of botulinum toxin, which inhibits acetylcholine release and leads to flaccid paralysis.

questions.stem: Father of medical microbiology:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Robert Koch

 

Robert Koch is recognized as the father of medical microbiology due to his pioneering work in identifying the causative agents of infectious diseases and establishing Koch's postulates, which are fundamental principles for linking specific microorganisms to specific diseases. His work on tuberculosis, anthrax, and cholera significantly advanced the field of medical microbiology, making him a foundational figure in this discipline.

 

Note:

 

 

Educational Objective:

 

Robert Koch is known as the father of medical microbiology for his contributions to identifying microbial causes of diseases and establishing foundational principles in the field.

questions.stem: A patient was exposed to hepatitis B infection. Which of the following markers will always be present irrespective of whether the patient recovers from the infection or not?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Anti-HBc

 

In the context of hepatitis B infection, the presence of specific antigens and antibodies helps determine the stage of infection and recovery. Here’s a breakdown of the relevant markers:

 

 

 

  1. Anti-HBc (antibody to hepatitis B core antigen):
    • Anti-HBc appears during the acute phase of hepatitis B infection and persists for life, regardless of whether the patient recovers from the infection or progresses to chronic infection.
    • It is present in both acute and past resolved infections, making it a reliable indicator of past exposure to the virus.
  2. HBsAg (hepatitis B surface antigen):
    • HBsAg is present during active infection, indicating that the virus is circulating in the blood. However, it disappears once the infection resolves and is replaced by Anti-HBs.
  3. Anti-HBs (antibody to hepatitis B surface antigen):
    • Anti-HBs indicates immunity to hepatitis B, either through recovery from natural infection or vaccination. It appears after HBsAg disappears, indicating recovery or immunity.
  4. HBeAg (hepatitis B e antigen):
    • HBeAg is a marker of viral replication and infectivity. Its presence indicates active viral replication, but it disappears once viral replication declines.

 

Anti-HBc, particularly the IgG type, remains in the blood for a lifetime after exposure to hepatitis B, making it the marker that persists regardless of the infection's outcome.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Anti-HBc is the marker that remains detectable in a patient who has been exposed to hepatitis B, regardless of whether they recover or develop chronic infection. It is indicative of past or present infection with hepatitis B.

questions.stem: HIV target binding site:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) gp120, gp41

 

The HIV virus has two key glycoproteins on its surface that are crucial for its interaction with host cells: gp120 and gp41. These glycoproteins facilitate the process of HIV binding to and entering host cells, specifically CD4 T cells and macrophages:

 

  • gp120 is responsible for the initial attachment of the HIV virus to the CD4 receptor on the surface of the host cell. This binding is essential for the virus to recognize and attach to the host cell, making it a critical part of the entry process.
  • gp41 plays a role after the initial attachment. It interacts with co-receptors (such as CCR5 or CXCR4) on the host cell surface, leading to the fusion of the viral envelope with the host cell membrane, allowing the viral RNA to enter the host cell.

 

Thus, both gp120 and gp41 are integral to the process of HIV binding and entry into target cells.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. gp120, p24: This is incorrect. While gp120 is involved in attachment, p24 is a core protein (part of the viral capsid) and does not play a role in the initial attachment process.

 

Option C. gp120: While gp120 is essential for attachment, gp41 is also required for the subsequent fusion, making this option incomplete.

 

Option D. p24, p40: This is incorrect because p24 is a structural protein that forms the viral capsid, and p40 is not directly related to the attachment process of HIV.

 

Educational Objective:

 

HIV utilizes gp120 for attachment to the CD4 receptor and gp41 for subsequent fusion with the host cell membrane, enabling entry into the host cell.

questions.stem: Culture media are sterilized by:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Autoclaving

 

Sterilization of culture media is a crucial step to ensure that no unwanted microorganisms are present before inoculating the media with a specific sample. Autoclaving is the most common method used for sterilizing culture media. It uses steam under pressure (typically 121°C at 15 psi for 15-20 minutes) to kill all microorganisms, including spores.

 

Autoclaving is effective for most culture media unless the media contains heat-sensitive ingredients like blood, serum, egg, or sugar. These ingredients can be denatured or degraded by high heat, so alternative methods like tyndallization may be used for heat-sensitive media.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Beta-radiation: This is used for sterilizing disposable medical supplies like syringes and plastics but is not used for culture media.

 

Option C. Hot air oven: This method is suitable for sterilizing glassware, metal instruments, and powders but is not effective for culture media due to the high temperatures required, which could degrade the media components.

 

Option D. Tyndallisation: This is used for sterilizing heat-sensitive culture media (like those containing blood or serum) that cannot withstand autoclaving. However, it is a more time-consuming process and is generally not the standard method for most culture media.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Autoclaving is the preferred method for sterilizing most culture media, using steam under pressure to ensure complete sterilization. For heat-sensitive media, alternative methods like tyndallization are used.

questions.stemHtml: Which of the following life cycle is shown below?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Diphyllobothrium latum

 

The life cycle depicted involves a fish as an intermediate host, which is characteristic of Diphyllobothrium latum, also known as the fish tapeworm. The cycle starts when humans consume raw or undercooked fish containing the L3 larval stage of the parasite. After ingestion, the larva develops into an adult tapeworm in the human intestine, where it matures and releases eggs. The eggs exit the human body through the stool and hatch in water, releasing coracidia (L1 larval stage). These larvae are then ingested by a small crustacean, known as a copepod, where they develop into procercoid larvae (L2 stage). When the copepod is eaten by a fish, the larvae develop into plerocercoid larvae (L3 stage), which is infectious to humans when consumed.

 

This lifecycle is typical of Diphyllobothrium latum, which is known for being acquired through eating raw or undercooked fish.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Echinococcus granulosus. Incorrect because its life cycle involves carnivores (like dogs) as definitive hosts and herbivores or humans as intermediate hosts, developing hydatid cysts, rather than involving fish.

 

Option C. Taenia solium. Incorrect because it is typically transmitted through pork and involves cysticercus larvae in pigs, not fish.

 

Option D. Clonorchiasis: (caused by Clonorchis sinensis) is incorrect because, although it also involves fish as an intermediate host, its life cycle differs in details, such as having snails as a primary intermediate host before fish.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Diphyllobothrium latum (fish tapeworm) is acquired through the consumption of raw or undercooked fish containing L3 larva. It is characterized by a life cycle that involves:

 

Definitive host → Man

 

  • 1st Intermediate host → Cyclops / diaptomus
  • 2nd Intermediate host → Fresh water Fish

questions.stem: Which of the following stimulates adenylate cyclase with G-protein coupled action?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Cholera toxin

 

The mechanism of action of different bacterial toxins can be classified based on their effects on cellular processes. Cholera toxin, produced by Vibrio cholerae, specifically stimulates adenylate cyclase through G-protein coupled action. Here’s how it works:

 

 

Cholera toxin binds to the GM1 ganglioside receptors on intestinal epithelial cells. Once inside the cell, it activates the Gs alpha subunit of the G-protein complex.

 

This activation leads to continuous stimulation of adenylate cyclase, resulting in increased levels of cyclic AMP (cAMP).

 

The elevated cAMP levels cause enhanced secretion of chloride ions and water into the intestinal lumen, leading to the profuse watery diarrhea characteristic of cholera.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Shiga toxin: This toxin, produced by Shigella dysenteriae, inhibits protein synthesis by targeting the 60S ribosomal subunit, leading to cell death. It does not stimulate adenylate cyclase.

 

Option C. Diphtheria toxin: Produced by Corynebacterium diphtheriae, this toxin inhibits protein synthesis by inactivating elongation factor-2 (EF-2). It does not interact with adenylate cyclase.

 

Option D. Pseudomonas toxin (Exotoxin A): Similar to diphtheria toxin, exotoxin A from Pseudomonas aeruginosa inhibits protein synthesis by targeting elongation factor-2 (EF-2). It does not affect adenylate cyclase.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Cholera toxin activates adenylate cyclase through G-protein coupled action, leading to increased cAMP levels and severe watery diarrhea, distinguishing it from other toxins that primarily inhibit protein synthesis.

questions.stem: Which antibody is most commonly produced in the secondary immune response?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) IgG

 

During the secondary immune response, which occurs after the immune system is re-exposed to an antigen it has encountered before, IgG is the predominant antibody produced. This response is faster and more robust compared to the primary immune response due to the activation of memory B cells. These memory cells recognize the antigen quickly and produce IgG in higher quantities, which provides long-lasting immunity and more effective neutralization of the pathogen. IgG is especially important for its ability to cross the placenta, neutralize toxins, and opsonize pathogens for phagocytosis.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. IgA: IgA is primarily involved in mucosal immunity, such as in the respiratory and gastrointestinal tracts, but it is not the primary antibody in systemic secondary responses.


Option C. IgD: IgD functions mainly as a B-cell receptor and plays a role in the initiation of B-cell responses, but it is not produced in large amounts during the secondary immune response.


Option D. IgM: IgM is the first antibody produced during the primary immune response, providing an initial defense against infections, but it is not the dominant antibody during subsequent exposures.

 

Educational Objective:

 

IgG is the main antibody produced during the secondary immune response, enabling a faster, stronger, and more specific immune reaction due to the presence of memory cells.

questions.stemHtml: Following Foley’s catheterization, a patient in the ICU developed a urinary tract infection (UTI). The catheter tip was sent for culture and grown on blood agar. The blood agar picture after 24 hours is shown. The most likely agent causing UTI is:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Proteus mirabilis

 

The blood agar image shows swarming, which is a characteristic growth pattern where bacteria spread across the surface of the agar in concentric rings. Swarming is typical of Proteus species, particularly Proteus mirabilis. This organism is known for causing urinary tract infections, especially in patients with indwelling devices like Foley catheters.

 

  1. Swarming appearance: Proteus mirabilis is notable for its ability to swarm on agar, producing a distinctive concentric ring pattern, as seen in the image.
  2. UTI association: Proteus mirabilis is a well-known cause of catheter-associated UTIs. It produces urease, which raises the pH of urine, potentially leading to the formation of kidney stones.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Escherichia coli: While E. coli is a common cause of UTIs, it does not produce the characteristic swarming growth seen in the provided blood agar image.

 

Option C. Pseudomonas aeruginosa: Pseudomonas can cause UTIs, especially in hospital settings, but it does not exhibit the swarming growth seen here.

 

Option D. Klebsiella pneumoniae: Klebsiella can also cause UTIs, particularly in hospital-acquired cases, but like E. coli and Pseudomonas, it does not display swarming behavior on agar.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The swarming pattern on blood agar is a hallmark of Proteus mirabilis, which is also associated with catheter-associated UTIs. This characteristic helps distinguish it from other potential UTI pathogens.

questions.stemHtml: Rearrange the sequence of hand washing:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) 1-a; 2-c; 3-d; 4-b

 

 

Handwashing technique as recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO). Here is the correct sequence of the handwashing:

 

  1. Step 1 (A): Begin by applying soap or hand rub and rubbing hands palm to palm.
  2. Step 2 (C): Rub the back of each hand with the opposite palm.
  3. Step 3 (D): Rub with fingers interlaced, focusing on in between fingers.
  4. Step 4 (B): Pay attention to rubbing the thumbs and the backs of the fingers on the opposite palms.

 

Following this sequence ensures thorough handwashing, effectively removing germs and contaminants from the hands.

 

 

 

Educational Objective:

 

Proper handwashing involves sequentially cleaning the palms, backs of hands, between fingers, and thumbs, following the WHO guidelines for effective hand hygiene.

questions.stem: Which among the following exists in yeast form at 37°C and hyphal form at 25°C?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Histoplasma capsulatum

 

Histoplasma capsulatum is a dimorphic fungus, meaning it can exist in two different forms depending on the temperature. At 37°C (body temperature), it exists in the yeast form, which is typical for infections in humans. At 25°C (environmental temperature), it grows in the hyphal (mold) form. This ability to switch between yeast and mold forms based on temperature is a key characteristic of dimorphic fungi, which include other species like Blastomyces dermatitidis and Coccidioides immitis.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Malassezia furfur: Incorrect because it exists as a yeast and is not classified as dimorphic.


Option B. Cryptococcus neoformans: Incorrect as it is primarily a yeast and does not exhibit temperature-dependent dimorphism.


Option C. Aspergillus: Incorrect because it is a mold and does not switch to a yeast form at higher temperatures.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Histoplasma capsulatum is an example of a dimorphic fungus, existing in yeast form at 37°C and hyphal (mold) form at 25°C, making it capable of adapting to both environmental and host conditions.

questions.stemHtml: Match the following:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) a-4, b-1, c-2, d-3

 

Segregation of biomedical waste using different types of containers and bags:

 

 

 

Yellow Bag: Used for chemical waste and body fluids. Hence, option a matches with 4.

 

 

Red Bag: Used for contaminated waste that can be recycled, such as gloves, plastic containers, and other non-sharp items. Hence, option b matches with 1.

Proper segregation of biomedical waste into appropriate containers and bags is essential for safe disposal, minimizing the risk of contamination and ensuring compliance with waste management regulations.

questions.stem: Auto-infection is not seen in:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) H. diminuta

 

H. diminuta does not exhibit auto-infection.

 

Auto-infection is a process where the host is re-infected by the same parasite without it leaving the body. It is a characteristic feature seen in certain parasitic infections where the lifecycle can continue within the same host. The mnemonic "CHEST" helps recall the parasites that can cause auto-infection:

 

  • C stands for Capillariasis and Cryptosporidium.
  • H represents H. nana.
  • E corresponds to Enterobius.
  • S stands for Strongyloidosis (Strongyloides).
  • T represents Taenia solium.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Auto-infection is seen in parasites like H. nana, Strongyloides, Enterobius, and Taenia solium, but not in H. diminuta.

questions.stemHtml: The following plate shows H. influenzae colonies. Which of the following is responsible for the phenomenon shown? -
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) V factor

 

The image depicts a phenomenon known as satellitism, which is characteristic of Haemophilus influenzae when grown on blood agar in the presence of another bacterium like Staphylococcus aureus. Here’s how the phenomenon occurs:

 

 

H. influenzae requires two growth factors: X factor (hemin) and V factor (NAD or nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide).

 

X factor is present freely in blood agar as it is released from red blood cells.

 

However, V factor is intracellular and is not freely available in the blood agar unless the red blood cells are lysed (as in chocolate agar).

 

Staphylococcus aureus can release V factor by lysing red blood cells or directly producing it.

 

When a streak of Staphylococcus aureus is placed on a blood agar plate, it releases V factor into the surrounding medium, allowing H. influenzae to grow in close proximity to the streak of S. aureus.

 

The colonies of H. influenzae appear larger near the streak where the V factor is abundant, and smaller further away, giving the appearance of "satellites."

 

This phenomenon is called satellitism and is specifically due to the requirement for V factor.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. X factor: H. influenzae requires X factor for growth, but this is not responsible for the satellitism phenomenon seen on blood agar when co-cultured with Staphylococcus aureus.

 

Option C. PRP antigen: The PRP (polyribosyl ribitol phosphate) antigen is a component of the capsule of H. influenzae type b but is not related to the growth phenomenon of satellitism.

 

Option D. All of the above: This is incorrect because the phenomenon is specifically due to the release of V factor by Staphylococcus aureus.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The satellitism phenomenon seen with H. influenzae growing near Staphylococcus aureus on blood agar is due to the release of V factor (NAD), which is necessary for the growth of H. influenzae alongside the freely available X factor.

questions.stemHtml: Identify the organism in the Gram staining slide picture.
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Neisseria gonorrhoeae

 

The image provided shows a Gram-stained slide. The presence of Gram-negative cocci, which appear as pairs (diplococci) within white blood cells, is characteristic of Neisseria gonorrhoeae. This bacterium typically appears as kidney-shaped or bean-shaped cells when observed in a Gram stain. It is an important pathogen known for causing sexually transmitted infections like gonorrhea. In the context of Gram staining, Neisseria species appear as Gram-negative (pink or red) cocci.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Staphylococcus aureus: This is a Gram-positive cocci, appearing in clusters. Unlike Neisseria gonorrhoeae, it retains the violet color of Gram stain and does not appear as diplococci.


Option C. Streptococcus pneumoniae: It is also a Gram-positive cocci but typically appears as lancet-shaped diplococci. It is violet or blue in color when stained, in contrast to the pink appearance of Neisseria gonorrhoeae.


Option D. Haemophilus influenzae: This is a Gram-negative bacillus, not a cocci, and appears as small rods rather than the diplococci seen in the provided image.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Neisseria gonorrhoeae is a Gram-negative diplococcus, often appearing as kidney-shaped cocci in pairs within white blood cells on a Gram stain. It is distinguished from other Gram-positive cocci like Staphylococcus and Streptococcus and from Gram-negative rods like Haemophilus influenzae.

questions.stem: Correct order of gram staining is:

options.label: A
options.text: Gent ion violet → Iodine → Carbol fuchsin

questions.answerText: Gent ion violet → Iodine → Carbol fuchsin
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Gentian violet → Iodine → Carbol fuchsin

 

 

The Gram staining procedure involves a specific sequence of steps to differentiate between Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria based on their cell wall properties:

 

  1. Primary Stain (Gentian violet): The first dye applied, which stains all bacterial cells violet.
  2. Mordant (Iodine): This is applied to form a complex with the gentian violet, creating a larger molecule that is more likely to stay trapped in the thicker peptidoglycan layer of Gram-positive bacteria.
  3. Decolorization (Alcohol or Acetone): This step removes the dye from Gram-negative cells with a thinner peptidoglycan layer, but the Gram-positive bacteria retain the violet stain.
  4. Counterstain (Carbol fuchsin or Safranin): This stains the now colorless Gram-negative bacteria pink or red while the Gram-positive bacteria remain violet.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The correct sequence of Gram staining involves applying gentian violet as the primary stain, followed by iodine as the mordant, and then carbol fuchsin or safranin as the counterstain after decolorization

questions.stemHtml: An adolescent girl is brought with fever and chills for 3 days. Examination reveals signs of dehydration (positive skin pinch test and dry oral mucosa). Peripheral blood smear picture is given below. Identify the species of malarial parasite:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Plasmodium falciparum

 

Image shows red blood cells (RBCs) with multiple ring forms inside a single RBC, characteristic of Plasmodium falciparum. This species of malaria is known for its ability to infect multiple RBCs, often leading to the appearance of multiple rings within a single cell. Additionally, Plasmodium falciparum exhibits a unique "headphone" or "accolé" form, where the trophozoites appear to merge together, which is another identifying feature seen in the smear. The clinical history of fever and chills aligns with symptoms of malaria caused by Plasmodium falciparum.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Plasmodium vivax: This species typically presents with a single ring form in each RBC. The trophozoites of P. vivax tend to be larger and more amoeboid in shape. It does not exhibit multiple rings in a single RBC as seen in this image.


Option C. Plasmodium malariae: Similar to P. vivax, P. malariae also shows single ring forms per RBC. Its appearance is more compact and less variable in shape than P. vivax, but it does not show multiple rings in one RBC.


Option D. Plasmodium ovale: Like P. vivax, P. ovale shows single ring forms in RBCs. It is also distinguished by the characteristic "oval" shape of infected RBCs, which is not seen in the provided image.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Plasmodium falciparum is identified by the presence of multiple ring forms in a single RBC and its characteristic "headphone" or "accolé" appearance in blood smears. This differentiates it from other malarial species like P. vivax, P. malariae, and P. ovale, which typically have single rings per RBC.

questions.stem: All of the following are spore-forming bacteria except:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Vibrio cholerae

 

Spore formation is a survival mechanism used by certain bacteria to endure extreme environmental conditions. The process allows the bacteria to form endospores, which are resistant to heat, radiation, and chemicals. Only specific genera of bacteria can form spores, notably Bacillus and Clostridium. 

 

Mnemonic to remember the spore-forming bacteria is BSC Chemistry, which stands for:

 

  • B: Bacillus species (e.g., Bacillus anthracis, Bacillus subtilis)
  • S: Sporosarcina
  • C: Clostridium species (e.g., Clostridium botulinum)
  • C: Coxiella

 

Vibrio cholerae does not belong to any of these categories, as it does not form spores, 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Clostridium botulinum: This is a spore-forming bacterium belonging to the Clostridium genus. It produces endospores, enabling it to survive in adverse conditions.


Option B. Bacillus anthracis: A well-known spore-forming bacterium, Bacillus anthracis forms spores that are highly resistant and have been studied for their role in bioterrorism.


Option C. Bacillus subtilis: This bacterium is also spore-forming, common in soil, and known for its ability to produce tough endospores.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Spore formation is a feature seen in certain bacteria like Bacillus and Clostridium. Vibrio cholerae does not produce spores, which distinguishes it from other options in this question. The mnemonic "BSC Chemistry" can help remember the key spore-forming genera.

questions.stem: Which is enrichment media?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Selenite F broth

 

Enrichment media are designed to support the growth of a specific organism while inhibiting the growth of others, which is particularly useful when isolating a pathogen from a mixture of microorganisms. A key characteristic of enrichment media is that it is typically liquid in form.

 

In this context, Selenite F broth is a liquid medium used for the selective enrichment of Salmonella species from clinical specimens, while inhibiting the growth of other bacteria present in the sample. It creates an environment that favors the desired pathogen, making it easier to isolate.

 

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Chocolate media: This is not an enrichment medium but an enriched medium. It is used to grow fastidious bacteria like Haemophilus and Neisseria by providing additional growth factors, but it does not specifically inhibit the growth of other organisms.


Option C. Meat extract media: This is a general-purpose media that provides nutrients for a wide range of bacteria but does not selectively enhance the growth of a specific organism. It is not considered an enrichment medium.


Option D. Egg media: This type of media is typically used for culturing mycobacteria, such as Mycobacterium tuberculosis. It is a solid medium, not a liquid one, and thus does not fit the definition of enrichment media.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Enrichment media are typically liquid media that contain substances promoting the growth of certain microorganisms while inhibiting others. Examples include Selenite F broth, Tetrathionate broth, and alkaline peptone water.

questions.stemHtml: A 23-year-old female presents with fever and altered sensorium for two days with rashes on legs as shown. Her BP is 70/50 mm Hg, and neck stiffness is present. Lumbar puncture reveals cloudy CSF with 4200 cells/µL, protein level 198 mg/dL, and glucose 21 mg/dL. Which of the following correctly describes the organism causing this condition?

options.label: B
options.text: Gram-negative diplococci, ferments glucose and maltose

options.label: C
options.text: Gram-positive cocci, catalase negative, bacitracin sensitive

options.label: D
options.text: Gram-positive diplococci (lanceolate), catalase negative, optochin sensitive

questions.answerText: Gram-negative diplococci, ferments glucose and maltose
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Gram-negative diplococci, ferments glucose and maltose

 

The clinical presentation suggests bacterial meningitis, characterized by fever, neck stiffness, and altered sensorium, which points to inflammation of the meninges. The presence of a purpuric rash and low blood pressure (indicating shock) suggests a severe systemic infection, often associated with Neisseria meningitidis:

 

  1. Neisseria meningitidis is a Gram-negative diplococcus known for causing meningitis, especially in young adults.
  2. It is associated with a characteristic purpuric or petechial rash due to disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) and sepsis.
  3. The cloudy CSF with a high neutrophil count, elevated protein, and low glucose levels is consistent with bacterial meningitis.
  4. Neisseria meningitidis can be differentiated from Neisseria gonorrhoeae based on its ability to ferment both glucose and maltose.

 

 

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Gram-negative diplococci (kidney shaped), oxidase positive: While Neisseria species are oxidase positive and can have a kidney-shaped appearance, this option is less specific than the one describing glucose and maltose fermentation, which is characteristic of N. meningitidis.

 

Option C. Gram-positive cocci, catalase negative, bacitracin sensitive: This describes Streptococcus pyogenes, which does not cause the described presentation of meningitis with a purpuric rash.

 

Option D. Gram-positive diplococci (lanceolate), catalase negative, optochin sensitive: This describes Streptococcus pneumoniae, another cause of bacterial meningitis but not typically associated with purpuric rash or DIC.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Neisseria meningitidis is a Gram-negative diplococcus that ferments glucose and maltose, commonly causing meningitis with symptoms like fever, rash, neck stiffness, and signs of septic shock (Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome).

questions.stem: VDRL is an example of:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Slide flocculation

 

The VDRL (Venereal Disease Research Laboratory) test is a slide flocculation test used for the screening of syphilis. Flocculation tests are based on the formation of visible clumps or floccules when the antigen and antibody interact. In the VDRL test, cardiolipin antigen reacts with antibodies (reagin) present in the serum of syphilis patients, forming visible clumps when viewed on a slide. This test is carried out on a glass slide, which makes it a slide-based method rather than a tube-based one.

 

 

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Slide agglutination: Involves the aggregation of particles, such as bacteria or red blood cells, due to the interaction of specific antibodies with antigens. However, VDRL is not an agglutination test; it specifically involves flocculation.


Option B. Tube agglutination: This method is performed in test tubes, not on slides, and is used for detecting antibodies against antigens in a liquid medium. Examples include the Widal test for typhoid fever, not VDRL.
 

Option D. Tube flocculation: This involves a reaction occurring in a test tube with visible clumping, but VDRL is not performed in a tube—it is conducted on a slide, making this option incorrect.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The VDRL test is an example of a slide flocculation test, used to detect syphilis by observing clumping reactions between cardiolipin antigens and antibodies on a glass slide. It differs from agglutination tests, which involve larger particles like cells or bacteria.

questions.stem: Oil paint appearance on nutrient agar is seen in:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Staphylococcus aureus

 

The "oil paint appearance" on nutrient agar is a characteristic feature of Staphylococcus aureus. This description refers to the shiny, smooth, and slightly oily texture of the colonies that resemble oil paint. This appearance is due to the production of a golden-yellow pigment by Staphylococcus aureus when grown on nutrient agar. The colonies can be smooth and glistening, which gives them their distinctive look.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Streptococcus pyogenes: This bacterium does not produce a shiny or oily appearance on nutrient agar. It typically forms small, translucent colonies on blood agar rather than nutrient agar.


Option C. Bordetella pertussis: This organism has a different colony appearance, often described as "mercury drop" on specific media like Bordet-Gengou agar, but not as "oil paint" on nutrient agar.


Option D. Haemophilus influenzae: This bacterium requires enriched media, such as chocolate agar, for growth and does not produce the characteristic oily appearance seen with Staphylococcus aureus. It is known for satellite growth around other organisms rather than forming shiny colonies.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The "oil paint appearance" on nutrient agar is a distinctive feature of Staphylococcus aureus due to its golden-yellow pigment production, making it different from other bacteria like Streptococcus pyogenes, Bordetella pertussis, and Haemophilus influenzae.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is true about Trichomonas vaginalis?

options.label: B
options.text: Twitching motility is seen on wet saline mount

options.label: C
options.text: Cysts are seen on wet saline mount of vaginal secretions

options.label: D
options.text: It is not a sexually transmitted infection

questions.answerText: Twitching motility is seen on wet saline mount
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Twitching motility is seen on wet saline mount

 

Trichomonas vaginalis is a parasitic protozoan that causes a sexually transmitted infection. The trophozoites of T. vaginalis are pear-shaped and possess five flagella, which contribute to their characteristic jerky or twitching motility observed under a microscope on a wet saline mount. This motility is an important diagnostic feature in identifying the parasite during a laboratory examination.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. It cannot be cultured: This statement is incorrect. Trichomonas vaginalis can be cultured using special media such as the Diamond’s medium. Although it is not the most common method due to the ease of diagnosis through wet mounts, culturing remains a possible option.

 

Option C. Cysts are seen on wet saline mount of vaginal secretions: This is incorrect because T. vaginalis does not have a cystic form. It exists only as a trophozoite, making it unique among protozoan parasites, which typically have both trophozoite and cyst forms.

 

Option D. It is not a sexually transmitted infection: This statement is incorrect as Trichomonas vaginalis is indeed a sexually transmitted infection (STI). It is transmitted primarily through sexual intercourse, infecting the urethra in males and the vagina in females.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Trichomonas vaginalis exhibits twitching or jerky motility on wet saline mount due to its five flagella and is an STD that exists only in trophozoite form, without any cystic stage.

 

Note:

questions.stem: Medusa head colonies on nutrient agar are seen in:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Anthrax

 

The "Medusa head" appearance refers to the characteristic colonies of Bacillus anthracis (the causative agent of anthrax) when grown on nutrient agar. The colonies appear as rough, curly, and interlocking filaments, resembling the hair of Medusa, a figure from Greek mythology known for her snake-like hair. This appearance is due to the chain formation of bacilli that produce filamentous structures on the agar surface. The interlocking and wavy nature of the colonies makes them look like the hair of Medusa, giving it this unique name.

 

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Pneumococcus: This bacterium does not produce the Medusa head appearance on nutrient agar. Instead, it forms smooth, mucoid colonies when cultured on blood agar.


Option B. Legionella: This bacterium requires specialized media such as charcoal yeast extract (CYE) agar for growth and does not exhibit the Medusa head appearance.


Option C. Brucella: The colonies of Brucella species are generally small, smooth, and non-descriptive, lacking the filamentous structure characteristic of the Medusa head appearance seen in Bacillus anthracis.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The Medusa head appearance is a classic characteristic of Bacillus anthracis colonies on nutrient agar due to the interlocking and filamentous nature of its growth, making it distinct from other bacterial species like Pneumococcus, Legionella, and Brucella.

Salmonella typhi has three primary antigens: H, Vi, and O. The schematic image labels each of these antigens based on their location:

questions.stem: Infection with Clonorchis sinensis is associated with an increased risk of?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Cholangiocarcinoma

 

Infection with Clonorchis sinensis, a parasitic liver fluke, is strongly associated with an increased risk of developing cholangiocarcinoma, which is cancer of the bile ducts. This association is due to the chronic inflammation and biliary epithelium damage caused by the presence of the parasite in the biliary system. Over time, the continuous irritation and inflammation can lead to malignant changes in the bile duct cells, leading to the development of cholangiocarcinoma.

 

Other Options:


Option A. Cervical cancer: Incorrect. Cervical cancer is primarily associated with infection by the Human Papillomavirus (HPV), not Clonorchis sinensis.


Option C. Gastric carcinoma: Incorrect. Gastric carcinoma is mainly associated with infection by Helicobacter pylori, a type of bacteria, not Clonorchis sinensis.


Option D. Bladder carcinoma: Incorrect. Bladder carcinoma is associated with Schistosoma infection, a different parasitic organism, rather than Clonorchis sinensis.

 

Educational Objective:


Clonorchis sinensis infection increases the risk of cholangiocarcinoma (bile duct cancer).

questions.stem: Which of the following laboratory tests is used to diagnose rotavirus diarrhea?

options.label: A
options.text: Antigen detection in the stool sample

questions.answerText: Antigen detection in the stool sample
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Antigen detection in the stool sample

 

The preferred method for diagnosing rotavirus infection is the detection of viral antigens in a stool sample using enzyme immunoassay (EIA) or rapid antigen detection tests. 

 

 

Other Options:


Option B. Antigen detection in blood: Incorrect. Rotavirus does not typically circulate in the bloodstream in quantities sufficient for antigen detection, so this method is not used for diagnosis.


Option C. Antibody detection in serum: Incorrect. While antibody detection can indicate prior exposure or immunity, it is not used for the acute diagnosis of rotavirus infection. The presence of antibodies would not confirm an active infection.


Option D. Light microscopy of stool specimen: Incorrect. Light microscopy is not effective for diagnosing rotavirus because the virus particles are too small to be visualized using this method. Instead, specific antigen detection is required.

 

Educational Objective:


The primary diagnostic method for rotavirus infection is antigen detection in the stool, which is especially important for diagnosing diarrhea in infants and young children.
